name: Literature
description: Literature is a highly intellectual team-based deduction game, similar to Go Fish or Authors, but significantly more complex. Popular in Indian schools and universities (often called 'Lit'), it requires players to recall every card asked for by every player. The objective is to correctly identify and 'declare' all six cards of a specific half-suit (e.g., Low Hearts A-6 or High Clubs 9-K) to score points for the team.

history.origins: Derived from the traditional game 'Authors', it was adapted and complexified in South Asia during the mid-20th century. The most likely place of origin based on reports is southern Indiaâ€”Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
timeline: 1940s: Played in Tamil Nadu and Kerala, India, as reported by players whose families played during this era.
1950s: Becomes a staple in elite Indian engineering and medical colleges.
1980s: Standardized rules for 6-player (2 teams of 3) Literature competitive play emerge.
1990s: Spread to North America through Indian students; known as 'Fish', 'Canadian Fish', or 'Russian Fish' in some circles.
Present: Remains a cult favorite among strategy game enthusiasts in India and the UK university circuit.
history.cultural: Commonly played during train journeys and late-night study breaks in India; it is seen as a game for 'brainiacs' and strategic thinkers. The no-note-taking rule emphasizes pure memory and mental agility.
history.evolution: The game evolved to forbid any physical note-taking, making it a pure test of mental 'active memory' and coordination. The name 'Literature' may have been chosen to reflect the relationship to 'Authors'â€”a game with special cards where players collect sets consisting of an author and their works.

setup.players: 6 or 8 players divided into two teams of equal size. Teams sit alternately, each player between two opponents.
setup.deck: Remove the four 8s from a standard 52-card deck, leaving 48 cards. These form eight 'half-suits' (also called sets or books).
setup.dealing: Shuffle thoroughly and deal all cards one at a time face down. For 6 players: 8 cards each. For 8 players: 6 cards each.
setup.equipment: Standard deck. No writing materials allowed.

rules.objective: Collect and claim more half-suits than the opposing team. Each claimed half-suit scores 1 point.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Asking**: On your turn, ask any one specific player from the OTHER team for a specific card. A question is valid ONLY if: (a) You ask for a specific card (by value and suit), (b) You have another card in that half-suit in your hand, (c) The player you ask holds at least one card, (d) You do NOT ask for a card that is in your own hand. 2. **Successful Ask**: If the asked player has the card, they pass it to you face-up, and you keep the turn, asking another question. 3. **Failed Ask**: If the asked player does NOT have the card, your turn ends and it becomes their turn to ask. 4. **No Teammate Asking**: You may NEVER ask a teammate for a card. All questions must be directed to the opposing team. 5. **Claiming**: If you believe your team holds all 6 cards of a half-suit, you may claim it on your turn by saying 'Claim' and naming exactly who has which cards. If correct, your team scores the half-suit. If you state the location of even one card wrongly, the half-suit is cancelled and neither team gets it.
keyRules: 48 cards total (no 8s). 8 half-suits: Low/High of each suit (2-7 and 9-A).
Must have another card from the half-suit to ask for a card.
Successful ask = continue turn; failed ask = turn passes.
Claim by naming exactly who has which cards in a half-suit.
Failed claim = half-suit cancelled (neither team gets it).
Game ends when all 8 half-suits claimed or no cards remain.

strategy.basic: Listen to every question. If Player A asks Player B for the 5 of Spades, you now know that Player A has at least one Low Spade (2-7) and Player B does NOT have the 5 of Spades. Memorize this information.
strategy.intermediate: The False Scent: If you have four cards of a half-suit, and you know an opponent is tracking you, ask for a card in a DIFFERENT half-suit where you only have one card. This confuses their tracking of your 'power' suits. Negative Inference: If Player A asks Player B for a card and B doesn't have it, and later Player C asks Player D for the same card and D doesn't have it, you know the card must be with one of the remaining opponents.
strategy.advanced: Declarer's Coordination: Don't declare too early. If you know your partner has the 9 of Hearts but you aren't sure about the 10, ask for the 10. Even if you miss, your partner now knows YOU have Hearts and can follow up. The 'Loaded Question': If you have 5 of the 6 cards in a half-suit, ask for the 6th card from an opponent who you suspect has it. If they give it to you, claim immediately. If not, you've learned who doesn't have it, narrowing down the location.
tips: Mentally 'label' cards. Spades 2-7 = 'Low Spades'. Spades 9-A = 'High Spades'. Never mix them up.
Track the count of cards each player has. Sudden drops indicate successful claims or many cards given away.
If an opponent asks for a card you have, note which teammate they were askingâ€”they may be coordinating.
Don't claim unless you're at least 90% sure. A failed claim gives the opponents a free half-suit.
The 8s are removedâ€”don't waste mental energy looking for them!

scoring.description: Each claimed half-suit scores 1 point for the claiming team.
scoring.winCondition: Team with the most claimed half-suits (out of 8) wins. In case of tie (4-4), the game is a draw.

synthesis.shortDescription: A team-based deduction game requiring perfect memory of every question asked, where players claim half-suits by knowing exactly who holds what.
